docs/quality/traceability.md|> Status: - Round 7: `policy make` and `sign --check` take the committed trust file and the three PEMs next to the template as defaults (overridable by flags), with the same trust-hash check, so the first signed rc-tag run's and Release's pinned lines pass no file flags. PR 1 writes the template and the verify side only; Release signing the finished policy (rule 57) is PR 4. Witness's stage records cannot go to Rekor (Witness has no Rekor support); they carry the timestamp authority's stamp and are kept as release evidence (rule 53b). Decisions: - Step-8 round 1: - (a) the certificate chain is checked against the policy's root ONLY (the system trust store is switched off with -no-CAfile -no-CApath -no-CAstore -trusted), and tested with an attacker CA in SSL_CERT_FILE and SSL_CERT_DIR; - (b) timestamps come in two forms, a bare token in Witness records (go-witness timestamp/tsp.go) and a whole DER TimeStampResponse in a Sigstore bundle (protobuf-specs sigstore_common.proto), read by their type; - (c) Rekor is pinned to v1 by .github/policy/cosign-signing-config.json (cosign v3.1.3 `--signing-config`, an advisor-visible change to the pinned cosign command line: the default would use the TUF signing config, which may name Rekor v2 with no signed entry timestamp), and the log key in the trust file is the v1 key only; - (e) a record with a repeated JSON key or any signature count but one is refused. - Step-8 round 2 (NB-1, Opus): the certificate field of a record, and the verifier of a Rekor entry's body, must be EXACTLY ONE certificate PEM block with nothing but whitespace around it and no bytes after the certificate's outer SEQUENCE; the identity is read from that one DER and openssl verifies a PEM re-made from the same DER (before this, text or base64 before a genuine block was skipped by openssl but read as the identity by the homemade DER reader, so a self-made certificate with the right identity placed before any genuine certificate was accepted); every JSON reader is UTF-8 only (UTF-16/32 are refused, not guessed). - `sign --check` and `check-build-record` take exactly one of --template (the committed template: the per-tag policy is made there from GITHUB_REF) and --policy (a finished policy); the stage-sign.yml line and its pin changed from `--policy <template>` to `--template <template>`. - The flag `--rekor-stub` keeps its name only because later pull requests (PR 2-4) pin lines against it; it names the file of Rekor entries a bundle carries. - Opus N-9 is left as a documented note (no change). - Step-8 round 3 (B-1, both seats): the time of a timestamp is read ONLY from the bare token that the timestamp authority signed (a whole response is first required to have a clean status, no status string other than the TSA default ("unspecified") and no failure info, and is then reduced to its token with `openssl ts -reply -token_out`; the TSA's signature is verified over that same token), because a response's status section lies outside the TSA's signature and an edited statusString `x\nTime stamp: <date>` used to set the time compared with the certificate's validity; the stamp form is bound to the record type (a Witness collection carries the bare token `tsp`, the provenance the whole response `rfc3161-response`; the signed release policy either, PR 4 decides) and a mismatch is refused; a genTime with milliseconds is read and the fraction dropped; a certificate with a repeated extension (a second SAN, a second Build Config URI) is refused; the DER reader is not a general parser and trusts only the structure of a Fulcio-signed certificate. - `actions` follows a listed local composite action wherever it is stored, including under .github/workflows/, and skips following only a reference that names a .yml/.yaml file (a reusable workflow, judged as a workflow of its own). - The token of the key and token attempts must name exactly <repo>/.github/workflows/stage-sign.yml@<ref> of this repository (GITHUB_REPOSITORY). - Codex security round 1 (Oct 10): - (S1) after cosign, `sign` refuses a bundle with no or an empty timestamp list or Rekor entry list, naming each, verifies the two files it wrote as stage sign and requires the payload cosign signed to be, as parsed JSON with exact types (true is not 1, 1 is not 1.0), the statement Sign built (Opus round-1 verify F1, H2) before it prints ok; --out must not exist yet (., a folder, a file or a symlink is a usage error before anything runs) and any refusal, or any failure of that self-check, removes only the files Sign wrote and the folder it made (H1); - (S2) a Rekor entries file whose `entries` is not a list of objects is a refusal, never a traceback; - (S3) base64 must be canonical (re-encoding gives the same text) and JSON readers refuse NaN, Infinity, -Infinity and numbers that overflow to infinity (1e400); - (S4) only `actions` imports PyYAML; the Sign path runs on the standard library. - Codex security round 3 (Oct 10): an envelope field of the wrong JSON type is a refusal, and the issuer (.1.8) and Build Config URI (.1.18) extensions must each be one DER UTF8String TLV (Fulcio's v2 OID specification). - Codex security round 2 (Oct 10): every certificate of the Fulcio chain and of the TSA chain is checked AT the stamp's authenticated genTime (openssl -attime at the whole second below it, never -no_check_time), so an intermediate or a TSA signer that had expired, or was not yet valid, then is refused; genTime keeps its fraction (12:00:00.5 is after a certificate ending 12:00:00; for the certificate window openssl's check at the whole second below already decides, the fraction decides the 10-minute allowance after the verification clock, and a case pins that); a Rekor entry's logIndex and integratedTime must be canonical decimal strings, which fits the protobuf-JSON Sigstore bundle (int64 as strings): the Rekor REST API writes these fields as JSON numbers, which are refused, so the later pull request that produces the --rekor-stub file must take the entries from the bundle or emit protobuf-JSON strings; `sign` with no cosign on PATH is a refusal that removes the output folder it made. - Advisor reading, Oct 9 (handoff 0334; the ratified text is unchanged): a stage's identity in rules 52/52a/57 is the certificate whose SAN (Build Signer URI) is the stage file at the tag AND whose Build Config URI extension (OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.18, the top-level workflow) is release.yml at the same tag, issued by GitHub's OIDC issuer; the policy pins all three. - Witness's own verify can check the issuer but not the Build Config URI (in-toto-witness options/verify.go:80-99), so bin/chain-verify.py checks it. Stated exclusions: - (d) the Rekor entry in the tests is SYNTHETIC but has the real fields (sigstore-go pkg/tlog/entry.go, protobuf-specs sigstore_rekor.proto, Rekor dsse 0.0.1); the first signed rc-tag run captures a genuine bundle to replace it, and confirms the cosign bundle shape and whether the issuer extension is .1.8 or .1.1; Open items: - OPEN until one genuine cosign v3.1.3 bundle is captured at the first signed rc-tag run (cutover checklist): the verifier requires BOTH a Rekor v1 inclusionPromise (signed entry timestamp) and an inclusionProof with a checkpoint signed by the same Rekor key (the entry is in the tree); an entry with only one of them is refused. The audit path and checkpoint code is run against a real public Rekor v1 dsse entry (read-only); a bundle written by cosign itself is not yet captured. - The OIDC issuer is read from OID .1.8; the spike certificate dumps list .1.1 and not .1.8, so the first signed rc-tag run must confirm .1.8 is present on a real certificate.

The owner's rule (ratified Oct 21 2026, ops/docs/ratify/2026-10-21-signer-builder-separate-jobs.md; "it can't sit on the same machine ... it violates nist 800-53 ... the signer and the builder need hardware isolation and the builds in general need hardware isolation ... the best github actions can do for that, assuming we use github hosted runners, is to use separate jobs in the workflow"): (1) a job that holds the signing key or any publish credential never receives a build output other than the exact artifacts it signs or publishes (Build's), so Rebuild's apks never reach it; (2) the byte comparison of Build's and Rebuild's apks runs in the compare job of the Release stage, which holds contents read only (no secret, no publish permission, no environment, no identity token) and runs as one plain step; it passes on only a small result file, which the verify job's release-verify step checks against Build's attested apk digests, and neither the verify nor the release job downloads a rapk; (3) each build (Build, Rebuild, each architecture) is its own job. The Build and Rebuild jobs mint no certificate and hold no identity token. The throwaway key is key hygiene and not the boundary: a step of the same job can read it, so a record made inside a build job is not unforgeable by itself. The guarantee is that Sign checks every product digest of a record against the artifacts it receives before it signs, and that every verifier refuses a record whose only signature is the throwaway key, a record under the former stage-build.yml or stage-reproducibility.yml identity, and any *.local.json; the product digests of Rebuild's apks are bound to the apks in the compare job of the Release stage (a mismatch is a refusal there), because Sign never receives them | ci-workflow | yes | approved | 6 item(s) |

docs/quality/traceability.md|Once a month the release chain drafts one letter that rolls up that month's public evidence, takes every line of it from release assets it has checked first, signs it with the KMS release key as a release artifact (its Rekor entry is recorded), and attaches it to a release; if any check fails, no letter is made and the job fails (owner DECIDED Oct 27 2026, ops/docs/ratify/2026-10-27-monthly-evidence-letter.md, rules 1 to 8 and the 23:20 amendment: fully automated, no per-month approval, the owner's typed name and title). Every piece of evidence stays public at every tier, so the letter is a public release asset too; it states public facts about published evidence and makes no promise beyond them. It lists the releases published that month, the patch releases and why, the VEX statements added, the Check records of each release, any advisory, and one line binding it to the version of the controls document in force. It is made by a template, never by a model.
